newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says no alternative to budget savings.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says no alternative to budget savings.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, introducing the 1997 budget for its first reading in parliament, said there was no alternative to his government's austerity policies.
"Only he who saves today can invest tomorrow," Waigel told deputies in the lower house of parliament. Further spending savings and tax cuts were needed to help create new jobs.

The conservative governing coalition's 1997 draft foresees spending of 440 billion marks, down 11 billion marks on this year. Borrowing should be cut to 56.5 billion marks from around 70 billion marks -- above target -- this year.
Waigel said that the government was determined to meet the Maastricht criteria covering government borrowing next year and qualify for planned European monetary union in 1999.

"We will stick to the key figures of the 1997 budget despite the risks from the labour market," he said. Waigel had to stump up 12.5 billion marks last week to cover the shortfall in state jobless benefits this year caused by unemployment near four million, but wants to avoid a repeat next year.

He also said that the German economy was showing a stronger recovery than earlier expected. He said that growth this year would exceed a government forecast of 0.75 percent and that an expansion of one percent was "achievable".
